## Learning objectives

By the end of this session, you will

- Understand the basic grammar and layered structure of `ggplot2`
- Identify common graph components and choose an appropriate chart type
- Create simple plots using data, aesthetics, and geometric layers
- Interpret the main elements of a `ggplot2` figure

We **DO NOT** expect:

- Memorize functions in the `ggplot2`

## Preamble

**About Ray's part**

I am responsible for introducing commonly used libraries in R. So most of the time we will keep using functions that are predefined by others. 

Questions that Ray could **barely** give you an explanation better than AI/documentation:
  
- "What does this function do" -> Go to find the documentation `?FUNCTION_NAME` or ask AI
- "Why is this named XXXX()" -> The developer named it that way

Questions and competency you need to develop:

- "Why we need to do this?"
- Describe the task so AI can help you generate code

# Installing packages

## Package

:::{.columns}
:::{.column}

- A package is a bundle of functions, data, and documentation. You can import them through

```R
library(package_name)
```

- while using functions under the package you can use

```R
package_name::function_name()
```
or

```R
library(package_name)
function_name()
```
:::

:::{.column}

- You can check what packages have been installed, imported to your environment using the tab `Packages`

![Checking packages](/assets/images/package/package.png){width=80%}
:::

:::
## Installing package

**Golden rule**: refer to the documentation of the specific package

-  CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network) (**Major package channel**)  

```R
install.packages("ggplot2")
install.packages("tidyverse")
```

-  Bioconductor (**Biomedical packages**)  

```R
BiocManager::install("DESeq2")
```

-  GitHub (**code at the developmental stage**)  

```R
devtools::install_github("tidyverse/ggplot2")
```


# ggplot2

## Introduction to ggplot2

**About `ggplot2`**

- Visualization library in R for creating elegant and complex visualizations. 
- `ggplot2` is part of the tidyverse collection of R packages.
- Developed by Hadley Wickham [@wickham2010layered]. He received the COPSS Presidents' Award for his contributions to the tidyverse collection.
- Flexible and intuitive once you understand its core concepts.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(ggplot2)
```
:::



## About the data

`iris` is a dataset introduced by Ronald Fisher in 1936 that collects iris flower morphology measurements from 3 species 

:::{.columns}

:::{.column}  

- `Setosa`, 
- `Versicolor` 
- `Virginica` 

it measures the length and width of iris's sepal and petal
 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
data(iris)
head(iris)
```

## Choosing the Visualization

:::{.columns}

:::{.column width=50%}

Thinking process and decision flowchart will help you determine which type of graph to use (at least within the scope of this course):

1. What is the purpose of displaying the graph?
2. What types of data are you going to present?

:::

:::{.column width=48%}


```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A{Data type} -->|Continuous| B{Purpose}
  A{Data type}  -->|Discrete| C{Purpose}

  B{Purpose}-->|Exploration| D((Histogram/Boxplot))
  B{Purpose} -->|Association| E((Scatter plot))
  B{Purpose} -->|Association+time| T((Line plot))

  C{Purpose}-->|Exploration| F((Bar chart))
  C{Purpose} -->|Association| G((Tree map))
```

:::

:::

## Overview of ggplot2 logics

:::{.columns}

:::{.column}

`ggplot2` is designed as if you are plotting by hand, so the process looks like

1. Defining coordinate systems
2. Plotting dots, lines, bars, and etc.
3. Adding legend and axis information

:::

:::{.column}

![Layer features of ggplot2](/assets/images/ggplot2/layer.png)

:::

:::

## Layer 1: Coordinate system

:::{.columns}

:::{.column width=40%}
First, we define the coordinate system for our `iris` data in R

The function is `ggplot()`, which takes two arguments ^[Actually, you can provide them in the later stage instead of here]

- `data`: The data you are going to use
- `mapping`: Should be wrapped in `aes()` specifying how each column maps to the coordinate. 
  
:::

:::{.column width=57%}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Initialize a ggplot object with 
# data and aesthetic mappings
p <- ggplot(data=iris, 
  mapping = aes(x = Sepal.Length))
p  # Display the base plot (no layers added yet)

# Alternative 
# p <- ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length))
# p
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Showing coordinate systems in ggplot2](ggplot2_files/figure-revealjs/fig-1-1.png){#fig-1 width=960}
:::
:::

:::

:::

::: .aside

:::

## Layer 2: Plotting data

::: {.columns}

:::{.column}

The general format for plotting items will be 

`geom_XXX(mapping=aes())`

In `aes()`, you can map anything to the figure, common terms could be 

- `x`
- `y`
- `color`, or `colour`
- `fill`, `shape`, etc.
:::


:::{.column}
These functions are named in the format `geom_XXXX`:

|                 |  Function name  | 
|-----------------|-----------------|
|    Histogram    | `geom_histogram()`   |
|    Box chart    | `geom_boxplot()`|
|    Bar chart    | `geom_bar()`    |
|  Scatter chart  | `geom_point()`|
|   Line chart    | `geom_line()`   |
:::


:::


## Layer 2: Example

:::{.columns}
::: {.column}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
p+geom_point(aes(y = Petal.Width, color=Species))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Scatter plot for Sepal length and Petal width](ggplot2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::

:::

:::{.column}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
p+geom_boxplot()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Box plot for Sepal length](ggplot2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::

:::

:::

- `+` operator to stack on the original `ggplot()`
- Adding additional mapping in the `geom_XXX()`
- Overwriting mapping in the `ggplot()`

## More examples


:::{.columns}
::: {.column}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data=iris)+
  geom_histogram(aes(x=Petal.Length, color=Species))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Histogram for Petal length](ggplot2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::

:::


:::{.column}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data=iris)+
  geom_bar(aes(x=Species,fill=Species))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Histogram for Petal length](ggplot2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


:::

:::

**Some notes** ^[If you find the figure behave not as expected. The best choice is always look up the documentation, or ask AI.]: `color` affects the border color (dots/lines), `fill` affects the rectangle color
  

::: .aside
:::

## Layer 3: Legends and axis


Scales are functions indicate how each variable behave and presents on the graph. The function usually in the format `scale_(AES)_(datatype)`:

|                 |         Discrete           |        Continuous        |
|-----------------|----------------------------|--------------------------|
|    X            |    `scale_x_discrete()`    |  `scale_x_continuous()`  |
|    Y            |    `scale_y_discrete()`    |  `scale_y_continuous()`  |
|  color          | `scale_color_discrete()`   | `scale_color_continuous()` |

:::{.columns}

:::{.column}

Most of the time you only need to handle the presentation in 
![Elements in the scale](/assets/images/ggplot2/fig_element.png)

:::

:::{.column}

| Argument name	  |     Axis     |   Legend  |
|-----------------|--------------|-----------|
| name            |     Label    |   Title   |
| breaks          |     Ticks    |    Key    |
| labels          |  Tick label  | Key Label |

:::

:::

## Example


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Create a scatter plot with customized axis and color legend labels
   p +
  geom_point(aes(y = Petal.Width, color=Species)) +  # Add points layer for data representation
  scale_x_continuous(name="Sepal Length") +  # Customize x-axis label
  scale_y_continuous(name="Petal Width") + # Customize y-axis label
  scale_colour_discrete(name="Species name")  # Customize color legend title
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Scatter plot of MPG vs cylinders with customized axis and legend labels.](ggplot2_files/figure-revealjs/fig-5-1.png){#fig-5 width=960}
:::
:::


## Save figure

:::{.columns}

:::{.column width=60%}

Add the function `ggsave("FILE_PATH+FILE_NAME.png")` after your ggplot instructions:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Saving plots as figure_theme_grey.png at the folder figure
ggsave("figure_1.png",p)
```
:::


- It supports most of the common image formats like `pdf`, `jpeg`, `png`
:::

:::{.column width=38%}

![Saved figure location](/assets/images/ggplot2/figure_loc.png)

:::

:::

## Final notes 

- There are far more things you can do in `ggplot2`
- Try to look up on the reference (or even use AI) when you need it.


# File structure

## Loading/saving data from folders

- By default, R sets the working directory to your `Documents` folder.
- Use `setwd(PATH/TO/NEW/WORKING/DIRECTORY)` to change the working directory.
- Use `getwd()` to see your current working directory.

Consider the following file structure

:::{.columns}

:::{.column}
```md
/ (root)
├── home
│   └── user
│       ├── documents
│       │   ├── course
│       │   │   ├── THIS_MARKDOWN.rmd
│       │   │   └── IMAGE.png
│       │   └── notes.txt
│       └── downloads
|           └── data.csv
└── var
```
:::


:::{.column}

There are two ways of specifying a path:

1. **Absolute path**
   The full location of the file or directory.
2. **Relative path**
   The location of the file or directory relative to the current directory.

:::

:::


##  Absolute Path

:::{.columns}

:::{.column}

```md
/ (root)
├── home
│   └── user
│       ├── documents
│       │   ├── course
│       │   │   ├── THIS_MARKDOWN.rmd
│       │   │   └── IMAGE.png
│       │   └── notes.txt
│       └── downloads
|           └── data.csv
└── var
```

:::{.callout-tip}
## Reminder for Windows system

- You will find your file path using `\` instead of `/` in your file explorer. In R, you need to transform these `\`s to `/` if you directly copy and paste the file path.
- You need to indicate your drive so it usually looks like `C:\Users\Ray\Blah\Blah`
::: 


:::


:::{.column}

**Absolute Path**

An absolute path starts from the root directory (`/`) and specifies the full path to a file or directory. 

- Path to `THIS_MARKDOWN.rmd`: `/home/user/documents/course/THIS_MARKDOWN.rmd`
- Path to `data.csv`: `/home/user/downloads/data.csv`

:::

:::




##  Relative path

:::{.columns}

:::{.column}

```md
/ (root)
├── home
│   └── user
│       ├── documents
│       │   ├── course
│       │   │   ├── THIS_MARKDOWN.rmd
│       │   │   └── IMAGE.png
│       │   └── notes.txt
│       └── downloads
|           └── data.csv
└── var
```
:::


:::{.column}

**Relative Path**

A relative path is defined relative to the current working directory. 

- `./` refers to the current directory,
- `../` means "go up one directory level".

:::

:::

Assume that we are working on `THIS_MARKDOWN.rmd`, so the current directory is `/home/user/documents/course`.

- Path to `IMAGE.png` : `./IMAGE.png` or `IMAGE.png`
- Path to `data.csv`: `../../data.csv`

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
